{{Short description|Definition and first properties of the Poisson-Dirichlet distributions}}

In [[probability theory]], '''Poisson-Dirichlet distributions''' are [[probability distributions]] on the set of nonnegative, non-increasing sequences with sum 1, depending on two parameters <math>\alpha \in [0,1)</math> and <math>\theta \in (-\alpha, \infty)</math>.

The Poisson-Dirichlet distribution can be defined as follows. Consider independent random variables  <math>(Y_n)_{n \geq 1}</math> such that <math>Y_n</math> follows the [[beta distribution]] of parameters <math>1-\alpha</math> and <math>\theta+n \alpha</math>. Then, the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution <math>PD(\alpha, \theta)</math> of parameters <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\theta</math> is the law of the random decreasing sequence containing <math>Y_1</math> and the products <math>Y_n \prod_{k=1}^{n-1}(1-Y_k)</math>.

This definition is due to [[Jim Pitman]] and [[Marc Yor]].<ref name=PitmanYor1997>{{cite journal
 |first1=Jim |last1=Pitman |first2=Marc |last2=Yor
 |title=The two-parameter Poisson&ndash;Dirichlet distribution derived from a stable subordinator
 |journal=Annals of Probability
 |volume=25 |issue=2 |pages=855&ndash;900 |year=1997
 |doi=10.1214/aop/1024404422
 |mr=1434129 | zbl = 0880.60076
|citeseerx=10.1.1.69.1273}}</ref><ref name=Bourgademaster>{{cite journal
 |first1=Paul |last1=Bourgade |title=Lois de Poisson&ndash;Dirichlet |journal = Master thesis}}</ref> It generalizes Kingman's law, which corresponds to the particular case <math>\alpha = 0</math>.<ref name=Kingman1975>{{cite journal
 |first1=J. F. C. |last1=Kingman 
 |title=Random discrete distributions
 |journal=J. Roy. Statist. Soc. Ser. B
 |volume=37 |pages=1&ndash;22 |year=1975}}</ref>

== Applications ==

=== Pitman-Yor process ===

The values drawn from this distribution can be used as weights for sampling an infinite sequence of discrete items, an instance of a [[Pitman–Yor process]]. This is used to model the observation process of words, or species, etc. It is useful because it can generate phenomena with [[heavy-tailed distribution]]s.

=== Number theory ===
[[Patrick Billingsley]]<ref name=Billingsley1972>{{cite journal
 |first1=P. |last1=Billingsley 
 |title=On the distribution of large prime divisors
 |journal=Periodica Mathematica
 |volume=2 |pages=283&ndash;289 |year=1972}}</ref> has proven the following result:  if <math>n </math> is a uniform random integer in <math>\{2,3,\dots,N\}</math>, if <math> k \geq 1 </math> is a fixed integer, and if <math> p_1 \geq p_2 \geq \dots \geq p_k </math> are the <math> k </math> largest prime divisors of <math>n </math> (with <math> p_j   </math> arbitrarily defined if <math>n </math> has less than <math> j </math> prime factors), then the joint distribution of<math>(\log p_1/\log n, \log p_2/\log n, \dots, \log p_k/\log n)</math>converges to the law of the <math> k </math> first elements of a <math> PD(0,1) </math> distributed random sequence, when <math> N </math> goes to infinity.

=== Random permutations and [[Ewens's sampling formula]] ===
The Poisson-Dirichlet distribution of parameters <math> \alpha = 0 </math> and <math>\theta = 1</math> is also the limiting distribution, for <math> N </math> going to infinity, of the sequence <math>(\ell_1/N, \ell_2/N, \ell_3/N, \dots)</math>, where <math>\ell_j</math> is the length of the <math>j^{\operatorname{th}}</math> largest cycle of a uniformly distributed permutation of order <math>N</math>. If for <math>\theta > 0</math>, one replaces the uniform distribution by the distribution <math>\mathbb{P}_{N, \theta}</math> on <math>\mathfrak{S}_N</math> such that <math>\mathbb{P}_{N, \theta} (\sigma) = \frac{\theta^{n(\sigma)}}{\theta (\theta+ 1) \dots (\theta + n(\sigma)-1)} </math>, where <math>n(\sigma)</math> is the number of cycles of the permutation <math>\sigma</math>, then we get the Poisson-Dirichlet distribution of parameters <math> \alpha = 0 </math> and <math>\theta</math>. The probability distribution <math>\mathbb{P}_{N, \theta}</math> is called Ewens's distribution,<ref name=Ewens1972>{{cite journal
 |first1=Warren |last1=Ewens
 |title=The sampling theory of selectively neutral alleles
 |journal=Theoretical Population Biology
 |volume=3 |pages=87&ndash;112 |year=1972}}</ref> and  comes from the [[Ewens's sampling formula]], first introduced by [[Warren Ewens]] in population genetics, in order to describe the probabilities associated with counts of how many different alleles are observed a given number of times in the sample.
